item.title: ChatGPT AgentForger, Hermes AI Misuse, Bing CVE-2026-32194/32191, and Golden Chickens
item.content:encoded:
Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Ministry — Should Read

A hacker used the open-source Hermes AI agent in unattended “YOLO” mode to automate post-exploitation activity inside Thailand’s Ministry of Finance after already gaining access. The key lesson is that self-hosted AI agents can quietly scale routine intrusion tasks without vendor oversight, while exposed logs and misconfigured services like HiveServer2 can reveal or enable the activity.

  • An operator installed the open-source Hermes AI assistant on a rented server, enabled its YOLO mode to remove approval prompts for risky commands, and pointed it at Thailand’s Ministry of Finance after already gaining access to the ministry’s network.
  • Hunt.io and researcher Bob Diachenko found the operator’s exposed Hermes logs on a web server with directory listing enabled, along with 585 files and 470 MB of attack tooling.
  • The Hermes agent performed repetitive post-exploitation tasks including kernel vulnerability scanning, LinPEAS runs, elevated-permission binary searches, filesystem listing, and recursive crawling of a ministry web root containing personnel records dating to 2012.
  • The recovered files included scripts targeting the ministry’s Hadoop cluster through HiveServer2, whose default authentication mode accepts any password, and a malicious Java add-on called HiveCmd.jar for running operating-system commands through database queries.
  • Nothing in the recovered material shows data leaving the network, and Thailand’s national CERT and cybersecurity agency were notified on July 15 but had not published anything by July 24 when The Hacker News checked.

Golden Chickens Resurfaces With Four New Malware Families and Modular Implants — Should Read

Golden Chickens (TAG-195) has resurfaced with four new malware families, including TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken, a modular ChonkyChicken variant, and ChromEggscalator. The shift to modular, operator-driven implants shows the MaaS ecosystem is actively evolving to improve flexibility and evade detection.

  • Recorded Future’s Insikt Group says the Golden Chickens malware-as-a-service operators, tracked as TAG-195, have resurfaced with four new malware families: TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken, a modularized ChonkyChicken variant, and ChromEggscalator.
  • Recorded Future said the four malware families share consistent command-and-control mechanisms, a shared persistence approach, string obfuscation, and execution through the same delivery model.
  • TinyEgg is a lightweight initial-access backdoor that provides host profiling, interactive shell access, persistence management, and can stop running if sandbox or automated analysis environments are detected.
  • ChonkyChicken expands on TinyEgg with browser credential theft, live browser session control through Chrome DevTools Protocol, credential-backed remote execution, network reconnaissance, and sustained surveillance.
  • The modular version of ChonkyChicken can fetch 14 different components from command-and-control infrastructure as needed, including modules for process management, screen capture, file manipulation, command execution, keylogging, audio capture, browser theft through ChromEggscalator, and persistence management.

ChatGPT AgentForger Flaw Could Deploy Rogue Workspace Agents via a Phishing Link — Should Read

Researchers disclosed AgentForger, a now-fixed ChatGPT Workspace Agents flaw that could let a phishing link silently create and deploy a rogue AI agent inside a victim’s organization using their existing app connectors. The agent could persist, run scheduled tasks, access sensitive workspace data, and act on attacker instructions without further user interaction.

  • Zenity Labs disclosed a critical vulnerability called AgentForger in OpenAI's ChatGPT Workspace Agents that could allow a phishing link to build, authorize, and deploy an attacker-controlled AI agent inside a victim's organization.
  • OpenAI addressed the AgentForger issue on June 8, 2026, following responsible disclosure.
  • The attack required a victim who was logged into ChatGPT, had access to Workspace Agents, and had at least one already authorized connector such as Outlook, Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Slack, or Teams.
  • The malicious link could cause ChatGPT Agent Builder to automatically execute a prompt from the URL, attach available connectors, disable approval prompts, publish the agent, schedule it to run hourly, and invoke Preview Mode to run immediately.
  • Zenity said the forged agent could persist inside the organization, receive tasks through emails with subjects beginning with “TASK,” access sensitive data through connected apps, report results to the attacker, and send phishing links through Teams as the victim.

Bing Images Flaws Let Crafted SVGs Run Commands as SYSTEM on Microsoft's Servers — Should Read

Researchers found that crafted SVG images submitted to Bing’s image search could trigger ImageMagick delegate command execution, running commands as SYSTEM on Windows workers and root on Linux servers. Microsoft fixed the two critical server-side flaws, but the case highlights the danger of letting untrusted image processing reach shell-enabled delegates or outbound network access.

  • XBOW found that a crafted SVG submitted to Bing’s image search could run commands as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on Microsoft’s Windows image-processing workers and as root on Linux workers.
  • Microsoft assigned CVE-2026-32194 and CVE-2026-32191 to the two flaws, rated both 9.8 on the CVSS scale, and fixed them server-side before the March advisories were published.
  • The two unauthenticated routes were the public Search by Image upload using the imageBin field to /images/kblob and the crawler route using the imgurl parameter, which bingbot/2.0 fetched into the same processing pipeline.
  • The exploit path involved an SVG image reference beginning with a pipe character that reached a delegate-enabled ImageMagick-compatible layer and was treated as a shell command rather than a filename.
  • The article recommends denying ImageMagick delegates in policy.xml, reducing accepted formats, reviewing delegates.xml, sandboxing conversion workers, reducing privileges, blocking outbound network access, and allowlisting server-side fetch destinations.

Europol flags 4,340 URLs for removal in 'The Com' crackdown — Should Read

Europol and investigators from nine countries flagged 4,340 URLs for removal in a crackdown on The Com, a decentralized extremist network linked to violent content, child exploitation, self-harm coercion, and cybercrime. The action builds on Project Compass, which has already led to 30 arrests and identified 179 suspects tied to the network.

  • Europol flagged 4,340 URLs for removal during a multi-week operation targeting online content linked to The Com, a loosely organized network of nihilistic violent extremist groups.
  • Investigators from Belgium, Finland, Hungary, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden took part in Europol’s Referral Action Days between June and July 2026.
  • Europol said The Com content included violent videos and images depicting self-harm, suicide, child sexual abuse material, animal cruelty, violent attacks, arson, and manuals on grooming, murder, improvised explosives, doxing, and swatting.
  • Project Compass, a yearlong Europol-led operation launched in January 2025, has resulted in 30 arrests and identified 179 suspects and 62 victims tied to The Com.
  • Europol describes The Com as a decentralized network whose affiliated groups recruit and groom victims through social media, messaging apps, and gaming platforms, coercing them into self-harm, violence, and production of child sexual abuse material.

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC Passed. The File Was Malware. — Should Read

A malicious spreadsheet was delivered from a genuinely compromised Microsoft 365 vendor mailbox, so SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and other authentication checks all passed. The key takeaway is that email authentication proves sender origin, not attachment safety, so trusted vendor emails still need file scanning and behavioral detection.

  • A hospitality and resort operator’s CEO received a short “please see attached” email from a real audiovisual vendor whose Microsoft 365 mailbox had been compromised.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC, and Microsoft compauth all passed because the message genuinely originated from the vendor’s legitimate Microsoft 365 tenant rather than a spoofed domain.
  • The email contained a roughly 138 KB spreadsheet named after the sending company, and file scanning returned a malicious verdict on the attachment.
  • The From and To headers both named the vendor’s own mailbox, while the real recipients were delivered by BCC, which the article describes as a classic sign of a compromised account blasting its contact list.
  • Themis flagged the message at 90 percent confidence and quarantined every copy across affected mailboxes before anyone opened the file.

Man gets six years for hacking 750 women's Snapchat accounts — May Read

An Illinois man was sentenced to more than six years in prison for phishing access codes to hack over 750 women’s Snapchat accounts, steal nude images, and trade or sell them online. Investigators also found he collected and distributed child sexual abuse material.

  • Kyle Svara, a 26-year-old Illinois man, was sentenced to 76 months in prison and three years of supervised release for hacking the Snapchat accounts of over 750 women to steal nude photos that he later traded or sold online.
  • Between May 2020 and February 2021, Svara targeted more than 4,500 victims by posing as a Snap Inc representative and using anonymized phone numbers to phish Snapchat access codes.
  • After stealing credentials, Svara accessed approximately 517 women’s Snapchat accounts without permission, downloaded nude or semi-nude photos, and activated two-factor authentication to lock victims out of compromised accounts.
  • Investigators found approximately 530 images and 600 videos depicting child sexual abuse material in Svara’s Mega account, and the Justice Department said he collected, distributed, and solicited CSAM.
  • Former Northeastern University track and field coach Steve Waithe hired Svara to hack Snapchat accounts of students and women’s sports team members, and Waithe was later sentenced to five years in prison for cyber fraud, cyberstalking, and sextortion.

The SOCI Act, explained: obligations, recent reforms, and where preemptive cyber defense fits — Optional

Australia’s SOCI Act requires critical infrastructure operators to register assets, report cyber incidents quickly, and maintain board-approved risk programs, with obligations expanding through recent and proposed reforms. The key takeaway is that early visibility into adversary infrastructure can help regulated entities manage risk before incidents occur and better meet SOCI’s tightening expectations.

  • Australia’s Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 applies to organisations that own, operate, or hold a direct interest in critical infrastructure assets across eleven sectors, including communications, financial services, data storage, defence industry, higher education, energy, food and grocery, healthcare, space technology, transport, and water.
  • For most responsible entities, the SOCI Act requires asset registration, cyber incident reporting within 12 hours for significant-impact critical incidents or 72 hours for lesser relevant incidents, and a board-approved Critical Infrastructure Risk Management Program covering cyber, physical, personnel, and supply chain risks.
  • Assets designated as Systems of National Significance carry Enhanced Cyber Security Obligations covering incident response planning, cyber security exercises, vulnerability assessments, and providing system information for a near real-time government threat picture.
  • The article says recent and proposed reforms have expanded the SOCI framework, including the ERP Act 2024, the Cyber Security Act 2024, and consultation on extending duties to third parties such as managed service providers and tightening supply chain expectations.
  • The article argues that Silent Push’s preemptive cyber defense can support SOCI obligations by mapping adversary infrastructure before attacks launch and issuing Indicators of Future Attack based on DNS, WHOIS, certificate, and hosting data.

Benchmarking report finds healthcare CISOs prioritize IAM, resilience as AI threats accelerate — Optional

Health-ISAC’s first CISO Benchmarking Report finds healthcare security leaders are prioritizing identity and access management and resilience as AI-amplified impersonation threats increasingly target help desks, finance teams, and clinical operations.

  • Health-ISAC released its first CISO Benchmarking Report based on survey responses from 76 healthcare chief information security officers.
  • The report found that healthcare CISOs are operating in an increasingly complex threat environment where cyberattacks can disrupt clinical care, jeopardize patient safety, and erode trust in healthcare institutions.
  • Survey respondents represented healthcare providers, payers, pharmaceutical companies, medical device manufacturers, and global operations.
  • The report covers cybersecurity priorities, leadership responsibilities, budgets, workforce challenges, framework adoption, and the growing role of artificial intelligence in the healthcare sector.
  • Health-ISAC Chief Security Officer Errol Weiss said AI-amplified impersonation beyond email is still underestimated in healthcare, including voice, video, and urgent workflow manipulation targeting help desks, call centers, finance teams, and clinical operations.

Seeing AI Agents Is Not Enough. Security Teams Must Enforce What They Can Do — Optional

Security teams should not stop at discovering AI agents; they need identity-centric, context-aware enforcement that controls what each agent can do based on ownership, permissions, usage, and intent. The key shift is from static inventories to consistent rules that govern agent actions across platforms.

  • The article argues that AI agent security is moving from adoption to visibility and then to control, with enforcement of least privilege becoming the central challenge.
  • Discovery alone is insufficient because AI agents can reason, plan, call tools, invoke APIs, access data, and take action without a human in the loop.
  • Security teams need to correlate agent ownership, consumers, identities, intent, access, usage, origin, and lifecycle before they can define meaningful controls.
  • The article says enforcement should govern what agents can do before, during, and after actions, rather than only remediating risks after they are detected.
  • The article calls for an identity-centric, context-aware, and platform-agnostic control plane that can discover, understand, and enforce rules for AI agents across enterprise environments.

2026 Mid-Year Update: On Pace for Our Biggest Year Yet — Optional

StepSecurity says it is on track for its biggest year yet, driven by rapid enterprise adoption and new products covering developer machines, CI/CD, package registries, and threat intelligence. The company frames this growth around AI-fueled software supply chain risk, arguing that organizations now need layered protection across the entire development pipeline.

  • StepSecurity says 2026 is on track to be its biggest year yet after more than 5x ARR growth in both 2024 and 2025.
  • The company says it closed roughly 7x more new customers in H1 2026 than in H1 2025, including publicly listed enterprises, unicorns, large-scale AI companies, and organizations in regulated industries such as financial services, defense technology, and healthcare.
  • StepSecurity says AI has increased both the amount of software being shipped and attackers' ability to target developer machines, code repositories, package registries, and CI/CD pipelines.
  • In H1 2026, StepSecurity shipped Harden-Runner for macOS and Windows, Dev Machine Guard for all three operating systems, Secure Registry, Device Policy, Secret Exfiltration Protection for GitHub Actions, and Threat Center API and threat intelligence feeds.
  • StepSecurity says its research team discovered or was among the first to publicly report several supply chain attacks in H1 2026, including the Axios npm compromise, the Shai-Hulud attack on TanStack, the Nx Console VS Code extension compromise, Microsoft's durabletask PyPI compromise, and Red Hat cloud services npm compromises.

N2K Cyberwire Daily – The defense against the AI arts. — Optional

Health-ISAC’s Errol Weiss appeared on the N2K Cyberwire Daily podcast to discuss healthcare ransomware trends and findings from recent Health-ISAC reports on CISO priorities and the sector’s threat landscape. The key takeaway is that healthcare cybersecurity depends heavily on strong information sharing, resilience, and collaboration as AI-driven threats accelerate.

  • Errol Weiss, Chief Security Officer at Health-ISAC, joined Dave Bittner on N2K Cyberwire Daily episode 2597 to discuss ransomware trends in the healthcare industry.
  • The episode also covers findings from the Health-ISAC 2026 CISO Benchmarking Report and Health-ISAC’s 2nd Quarter Heartbeat Report, which examine the current threat landscape facing the health sector.
  • The podcast episode begins with recent cyber news, and the guest segment with Errol Weiss starts at section 15:40.
  • Errol Weiss said the spirit and level of information sharing in the health sector is even better than what he saw in the financial sector.
  • The article links to the N2K Cyberwire podcast episode and related Health-ISAC resources and reports.
